idiom_name: typed loan with release() in finally; using/Disposable (TS 5.2+) where available
implementation_notes: TypeScript adds no runtime behaviour, so the hand-back is either the explicit release() in a finally block or the TypeScript 5.2+ using declaration, whose Symbol.dispose method runs at scope exit (the release notes introduce the Disposable, AsyncDisposable and DisposableStack types, plus SuppressedError). What the type system can do is make the contract visible: return a branded handle type whose only release path is the owner's method and keep the raw resource out of the public surface, because structural typing cannot distinguish 'borrowed' from 'owned' without a brand. The classic wrapper-owns-the-resource structure is replaced by using/DisposableStack plus the branded handle, and stays justified when the target runtime cannot be polyfilled.
pitfalls: using needs TypeScript 5.2+ and runtime support (Symbol.dispose, DisposableStack and SuppressedError are often polyfilled), and await using needs Symbol.asyncDispose; older targets silently degrade to try/finally discipline.

Structural typing cannot express ownership: any object with a compatible shape satisfies the loan interface, so brand the handle (unique symbol) or keep the constructor private to stop values from the wrong source type-checking.
Acquisition before the first await in an async API leaks when the caller never awaits the promise; keep the checkout inside the async function whose finally owns the release.
